title: Strings, part 1
goal: Tell string literals from char arrays, walk a string with a pointer, and use strlen, strcpy, strcat and strcmp safely, with buffers that always have room for the '\0'.

topics.title: String literals versus char arrays
topics.examNote: Short answers often ask what `sizeof` and `strlen` give for a string, or what is wrong with a line like `char *p = "hello"; p[0] = 'H';` or `s = "hello";`. Know the difference between an array that *holds* the characters and a pointer that *points at* a literal.

blocks.text:
### Quick review from Day 3

A C string is a `char` array whose end is marked by the **null terminator** `'\0'` (value 0, not the digit `'0'`, which is 48). `strlen` counts the characters before the first `'\0'`. A string of length `n` needs `n + 1` chars.

Today we look more closely at what the terminator means, at **string literals**, and at the two ways of naming a string: `char s[]` and `char *p`. You will use pointers (Days 11 and 12) all the time: a string is just an array, so `s + 4` and `*p` work exactly as they did on `int` arrays.

### Forgetting the terminator

The notebook's `missing_terminator.c` makes two arrays with `{'a', 'b', 'c', 'd'}`: four characters and **no** `'\0'`. These are arrays of `char`, but they are **not strings**. When `printf("%s", s1)` reaches the end of `s1` it does not stop; it keeps reading whatever bytes come next in memory until it happens to find a 0. That is **undefined behaviour**: on one run on our machine it printed `s1 = abcdabcd` (it ran on into `s2`), but another compiler or machine can print something else, or crash.

### The first `'\0'` ends the string

The terminator does not have to be the last element of the array, and an array can hold several. A string runs from where you start to the **first** `'\0'` after that. Because an array name acts as a pointer to element 0 (Day 12), `s + 4` is a pointer to element 4, and you can print the string that starts there:

blocks.caption: multiple_terminators.c (from the notebook)

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o multiple_terminators multiple_terminators.c
$ ./multiple_terminators
s     = abc
s + 4 = def
s + 8 = ghi

blocks.text:
### String literals

A **string literal** is characters between double quotes, like `"abc"`. The compiler adds a `'\0'` at the end for you, so the literal is an array of `strlen + 1` chars. It does this even if you write `\0` inside the quotes yourself (that is the notebook's "weird" example):

blocks.caption: literal.c (the notebook prints with %lu; we use %zu for size_t)

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o literal literal.c
$ ./literal
size   : 4
length : 3
size   : 8
length : 3
blocks.caption: `"abc\0def"` is 7 characters plus the added '\0': size 8. strlen stops at the first '\0': length 3.

blocks.text:
### Literals are read-only

A literal has **static storage duration** (Day 7): it exists for the whole run of the program, like a global. That is why the notebook's `hello()` may return `"HELLO"`: the literal does not die when the function returns (unlike a local array).

But the C standard says that **changing a literal is undefined behaviour**. Treat every literal as read-only. On Linux, literals are stored in memory the program may not write to, so the notebook's `literal2.c` (with the `str[0] = 'h';` line uncommented) usually crashes:

blocks.code:
char *str = "HELLO";   // str points at the literal itself
str[0] = 'h';          // undefined behaviour: tries to change the literal
blocks.caption: Compiles with no warning, even with -Wall. On one run on our machine it printed HELLO and then "Segmentation fault".

blocks.text:
### `char s[] = "..."` makes your own copy

When a literal **initialises an array**, its characters (with the `'\0'`) are **copied** into the new array. Now there are two independent copies. The literal is still read-only, but the array is yours, so you may change it (`literal3.c`: `char str[] = "hello"; str[0] = 'H';` prints `Hello`).

So there are two very different declarations:

| | `char arr[] = "cat";` | `char *ptr = "dog";` |
|---|---|---|
| what it is | an array of 4 chars holding a copy | a pointer (8 bytes) to the literal |
| `sizeof` | 4 (the whole array) | 8 (the size of a pointer) |
| `strlen` | 3 | 3 |
| change a char (`[0] = 'b'`) | OK | undefined behaviour |
| make it name another string (`= "cow"`) | compile error: no array assignment | OK: the pointer now points elsewhere |

blocks.caption: arr_vs_ptr.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o arr_vs_ptr arr_vs_ptr.c
$ ./arr_vs_ptr
sizeof(arr) = 4, strlen(arr) = 3
sizeof(ptr) = 8, strlen(ptr) = 3
arr = bat
ptr = cow

blocks.text: `sizeof` on a `char *` gives the size of the **pointer** (8 on our machines), not the length of the string. Use `strlen` for the length. The same is true inside a function with a parameter `char s[]` or `char *s`: it is a pointer (Day 5), so `sizeof(s)` is 8.

blocks.q: Why does `p = "cow";` compile when `arr = "cow";` does not?
blocks.a: `p` is a pointer variable: assigning to it just stores a new address (the address of the literal `"cow"`). `arr` is an array, and C has no array assignment (Day 3). To put new characters into an array you must copy them, for example with `strcpy` (next lesson).

blocks.q: `char a[10] = "hi";` What are `sizeof(a)` and `strlen(a)`? May you write `a[0] = 'H';`?
blocks.a: `sizeof(a)` is 10 (the capacity you asked for; the unused chars are set to 0). `strlen(a)` is 2. Yes: `a` is an array initialised with a copy, so it can be changed.

blocks.text:
### Key points

- A string ends at the **first** `'\0'` from where you start; `s + 4` is the string starting at index 4.
- A `char` array without a `'\0'` is not a string; printing it with `%s` is undefined behaviour.
- A literal `"abc"` is a read-only array of 4 chars (the compiler adds `'\0'`) with static storage duration.
- `char s[] = "abc";` copies the literal into your own array (changeable, `sizeof` 4). `char *p = "abc";` only points at the literal (do not change it; `sizeof(p)` is 8).
- Changing a literal is undefined behaviour (often a segmentation fault). Arrays cannot be assigned; pointers can.

topics.title: Walking a string; strlen and strcpy; buffer sizes
topics.examNote: Handwritten code often asks you to write a string function yourself (a `strlen` or `strcpy` with a pointer loop), and markers check the `'\0'`: the loop stops at it, and a copy writes it at the end. Every buffer needs room for `strlen + 1` chars.

blocks.text:
### Reading the prototypes in `<string.h>`

The string functions are declared in `<string.h>`. The notebook gives their **prototypes** (declarations):

```c
size_t strlen(const char *str);
char *strcpy(char *dest, const char *src);
```

`const char *str` means "a pointer to `char`s that this function will **not change**" (Day 2's `const`, now in front of what the pointer points at). You can pass any string: an array, a pointer, a literal, or `argv[i]`. A plain `char *dest` means the function **writes** into that memory, so it must be a real, big-enough, changeable array.

### Walking a string with a pointer

On Day 3 you looped with an index: `for (size_t i = 0; s[i] != '\0'; i++)`. With a pointer, start `p` at the string and move it one char at a time until `*p` is the terminator. You do **not** need the length first: the `'\0'` tells you where to stop.

blocks.caption: walk.c: count a character by walking a pointer

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o walk walk.c
$ ./walk
s: 4
p: 2
s from index 4: 2
z: 0
blocks.caption: `word + 4` points at the second "i": the function only sees "issippi". The empty string "" is just a '\0', so the loop body never runs.

blocks.text:
### How `strlen` works

There is no way to ask C how long an array is, so `strlen` must walk to the `'\0'` and count. The notebook shows three versions. Here is the pointer one: move `p` to the terminator, then the length is `p - str` (pointer subtraction gives the number of elements between, Day 12).

blocks.caption: mylen.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o mylen mylen.c
$ ./mylen
5
0
3

blocks.text: Another notebook version is `while (*str++ != '\0') { i++; }`. `*str++` means `*(str++)`: use the char `str` points at, then move `str` forward. It is short but easy to misread; the longer form above is fine on an exam. Undefined behaviour results if the string has no `'\0'` or the pointer is `NULL`.

### `strcpy`: copying a string

Arrays cannot be assigned (`s = "hello";` is a compile error), so to copy a string you call

```c
char *strcpy(char *dest, const char *src);
```

It copies the characters of `src` **including the `'\0'`** into `dest`, and returns `dest` (so you can pass the result straight to `printf`). `dest` must have room for `strlen(src) + 1` chars. The notebook's `copy.c` shows four uses:

blocks.caption: copy.c (from the notebook)

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o copy copy.c
$ ./copy
src   = 01234
dest1 = 01234
dest2 = 01234
dest3 = abcde01234
dest4 = 220
blocks.caption: dest3: copying to `dest3 + len` (index 5) overwrites "-----" and the copied '\0' ends the string. dest4: `s + 4` is "220", 3 chars plus '\0' = exactly 4.

blocks.text:
The behaviour of `strcpy` is **undefined** if:

- `dest` is not large enough, or
- the two strings overlap, or
- `dest` is not a char array or `src` is not a null-terminated string.

`strcpy` cannot check the size: it only receives a pointer. Making `dest` big enough is **your** job.

### Too small: why `too_small.c` is undefined behaviour

`too_small.c` (the notebook calls it `buffer_overrun.c`) uses a struct (Day 13) holding `char s[4];` and then `int i;`. It stores `'a'`, `'b'`, `'c'`, `'d'` in `s[0]` to `s[3]` and then writes `tmp.s[4] = '\0';`. But `s` has only indexes 0 to 3: the string "abcd" needs **5** chars. Writing to `s[4]` is out of bounds, which is undefined behaviour. One run on our machine:

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o too_small too_small.c
$ ./too_small
tmp.s = 
tmp.i = 99
tmp.s = abcd
tmp.i = 0
blocks.caption: Nobody assigned to tmp.i, yet it changed from 99 to 0: the '\0' landed in the first byte of i, which sits right after s in memory. No warning at all with plain -Wall (gcc -Wall -O2 does warn "array subscript 4 is above array bounds").

blocks.text: This is the dangerous kind of bug: no crash and no message, just a **different variable** silently changed. Another compiler could place things differently and give a different result. The same thing happens with `strcpy(dest, src)` when `dest` is too small, because `strcpy` always writes the `'\0'`.
Sizing a copy as `char dest[strlen(src)];` forgets the terminator. It must be `char dest[strlen(src) + 1];`. The program may even seem to work, because undefined behaviour does not have to crash.

blocks.q: `char *s = "CISC220";` How big must `dest` be for `strcpy(dest, s + 2);`? What does `dest` hold afterwards?
blocks.a: `s + 2` is "SC220": 5 chars, so `dest` needs at least 6. Afterwards it holds "SC220" followed by '\0'.

blocks.text: Copy `copy.c` into a file, change `char dest4[4];` to `char dest4[3];`, and compile with `gcc -std=c17 -Wall` and then with `gcc -std=c17 -Wall -O2`. Notice when you get a warning. Then put it back: the warning (when you get one) is about real undefined behaviour.

### Key points

- `const char *s` in a prototype: the function reads the string and does not change it.
- Walk a string with `for (const char *p = s; *p != '\0'; p++)`; the `'\0'` tells you when to stop.
- `strlen` walks to the `'\0'`; a pointer version returns `p - str`.
- `strcpy(dest, src)` copies including the `'\0'` and returns `dest`; `dest` needs `strlen(src) + 1` chars. `strcpy(dest + k, src)` copies into the middle; `src + k` copies the end of a string.
- Arrays cannot be assigned: use `strcpy`. Writing past the end of an array (too_small.c) is undefined behaviour and can silently change other variables.

topics.title: strcat and strcmp
topics.examNote: Fall 2014 Q4 explained the danger of `strcat` (the destination may be too small for the joined string) and asked for a safer alternative. Fall 2016 Q4 asked for a whole program that checks whether lines are in alphabetical order with `strcmp` and prints the first pair out of order. The faded and blank writing items below are modeled on these two (new details, no files or heap yet).

blocks.text:
### `strcat`: adding a string to the end of another

```c
char *strcat(char *dest, const char *src);
```

`strcat` ("string concatenate") finds the `'\0'` of `dest`, copies `src` there (including its `'\0'`), and returns `dest`. Both must already be proper strings. `dest` must be big enough for the **joined** string: `strlen(dest) + strlen(src) + 1` chars.

blocks.caption: concat.c (from the notebook)

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o concat concat.c
$ ./concat
s = 0123456789
blocks.caption: 5 + 5 characters + '\0' = 11: exactly enough.

blocks.text: Because `strcat` returns `dest`, calls can be **nested**: the inner call runs first.

blocks.caption: cat3.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o cat3 cat3.c
$ ./cat3
Ada 
Ada Lovelace (length 12, capacity 20)

blocks.text:
The behaviour of `strcat` is undefined if:

- `dest` is not large enough for the joined string, or
- the strings overlap (so `strcat(s, s)` cannot be used to join a string with itself), or
- `dest` or `src` is not a null-terminated string.

This is the danger the Fall 2014 final described: `char s1[10] = "Happy ";` has room for its own 6 chars, but `strcat(s1, "Holidays")` needs 6 + 8 + 1 = 15. It may crash, or silently overwrite other variables, just like too_small.c. A safe program **checks the lengths first** and only then calls `strcat`.
`char s[] = "01234";` has capacity **6**, exactly enough for itself. There is no room to `strcat` anything onto it. Give the array an explicit, large enough size: `char s[11] = "01234";`.

### `strcmp`: comparing strings

`==` on two arrays or pointers compares **addresses**, not characters. Two arrays holding "hi" are different objects, so `a == b` is false; gcc -Wall even warns:

blocks.caption: With `char *` it warns about a literal: `argv[1] == "yes"` gives "comparison with string literal results in unspecified behavior".

blocks.text:
To compare characters use

```c
int strcmp(const char *lhs, const char *rhs);
```

It is like Java's `compareTo`. It compares char by char until two differ (or both end). The result is:

- **negative** if `lhs` comes before `rhs`,
- **positive** if `lhs` comes after `rhs`,
- **0** if they are equal.

Only the **sign** is guaranteed, so test `strcmp(s, t) == 0`, `< 0` or `> 0`; never `== -1` or `== 1`. Equal strings: `strcmp(s, t) == 0`. Different: `strcmp(s, t) != 0`.

The order is the order of the character codes (Day 5), so:

- all uppercase letters come before all lowercase ones: `"Zebra"` comes before `"apple"`;
- a string comes before any longer string that starts with it: `"car"` before `"cart"` (its `'\0'`, value 0, is smaller than `'t'`);
- digits are compared as characters: `"10"` comes before `"9"` (`'1'` < `'9'`).

blocks.caption: compare.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -std=c17 -Wall -o compare compare.c
$ ./compare apple banana
apple comes before banana
$ ./compare apple Apple
apple comes after Apple
$ ./compare car cart
car comes before cart
$ ./compare 10 9
10 comes before 9
$ ./compare hi hi
hi and hi are equal

blocks.a: (a) true: "pea" is a start of "peach". (b) false: 'B' (66) is less than 'a' (97), so "Bob" comes first and the result is negative. (c) true.

blocks.text: Type in compare.c and run it with your own pairs: two words that differ only in case, a word and its plural, `""` and `a`. Predict each answer before you press Enter.

### Key points

- `strcat(dest, src)` appends `src` at `dest`'s `'\0'` and returns `dest`; `dest` needs `strlen(dest) + strlen(src) + 1` chars. Check lengths first: overflow is undefined behaviour (Fall 2014 Q4).
- Never `strcat` (or `strcpy`) a string onto itself: overlapping strings are undefined behaviour.
- `==` compares addresses. Compare characters with `strcmp`: negative (before), 0 (equal), positive (after). Test only the sign.
- Order follows character codes: uppercase before lowercase, a prefix before the longer string, `"10"` before `"9"`.

flashcards.front: What does `printf("%s", s)` do if the char array `s` has no `'\0'`?
flashcards.back: Undefined behaviour: it keeps reading past the end of the array until it happens to find a 0 byte. The output (or a crash) is not predictable.
`sizeof(s)` is 6 (5 written characters plus the '\0' the compiler adds). `strlen(s)` is 2 (it stops at the first '\0').

flashcards.front: What is a string literal, and how long does it live?
flashcards.back: Characters in double quotes, e.g. `"abc"`: a read-only array of `strlen + 1` chars (the compiler adds `'\0'`). It has static storage duration: it exists for the whole program.

flashcards.front: Is it legal to change a string literal through a pointer: `char *p = "hi"; p[0] = 'H';`?
flashcards.back: No: changing a literal is undefined behaviour (on Linux it usually crashes with a segmentation fault). Use an array instead: `char p[] = "hi";`.
`a` is your own 4-char array holding a copy (changeable, `sizeof` 4, cannot be assigned). `p` is a pointer to the read-only literal (`sizeof` 8, do not change the chars, but `p = "dog";` is fine).
`def`. `s + 4` points at index 4, and the string runs to the next `'\0'`.

flashcards.front: What does `const char *s` mean in a function's parameter list?
flashcards.back: `s` points at chars the function promises not to change. You may pass any string (array, pointer, literal, argv[i]).

flashcards.front: Write a loop header that walks a string `s` with a pointer.
flashcards.back: `for (const char *p = s; *p != '\0'; p++)` (or `char *p` if you will change the chars).

flashcards.front: How can a pointer version of `strlen` compute the length once `p` has reached the `'\0'`?
flashcards.back: `return p - str;`: pointer subtraction gives the number of chars between the start and the terminator.

flashcards.front: What does `strcpy(dest, src)` copy and return?
flashcards.back: All the characters of `src` **including the '\0'**, into `dest`; it returns `dest`.

flashcards.front: How big must `dest` be for `strcpy(dest, src)`?
flashcards.back: At least `strlen(src) + 1` chars. `strcpy` cannot check: too small is undefined behaviour.

flashcards.front: Why is `char s[100]; s = "hello";` an error, and what is the fix?
flashcards.back: C has no array assignment. Use `strcpy(s, "hello");`.

flashcards.front: What went wrong in too_small.c (`char s[4]` followed by `int i` in a struct, then `s[4] = '\0'`)?
flashcards.back: "abcd" needs 5 chars but `s` has 4. `s[4]` is out of bounds (undefined behaviour); on our machine the '\0' overwrote part of `i`, changing it from 99 to 0 with no error.
It must already be a string (have a '\0') and have room for `strlen(dest) + strlen(src) + 1` chars. It must not overlap `src`.

flashcards.front: Why not test two strings with `s == t`?
flashcards.back: `==` compares addresses (are they the same object?), not characters. Use `strcmp(s, t) == 0`.

flashcards.front: What can you rely on about the value of `strcmp(a, b)`?
flashcards.back: Only its sign: negative if `a` comes first, 0 if equal, positive if `a` comes after. Never test `== 1` or `== -1`.

flashcards.front: Does "Zoo" come before "apple" with `strcmp`? Does "10" come before "9"?
flashcards.back: Yes to both: strcmp compares character codes, and 'Z' (90) < 'a' (97), '1' (49) < '9' (57).

quiz.explain: `a` is an array of 6 chars (5 + '\0'); its length is 5. `b` has the capacity you asked for, 10, but holds "hi" (length 2). `c + 2` points at the "r" of "world", so the string is "rld": length 3.

Each `%s` stops at the first '\0' after its start. Index 3 and index 7 hold '\0', so `s + 4` is "two" and `s + 8` is "three". The literal has 3 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 5 = 13 written chars plus the added '\0': `sizeof` 14.

quiz.answer: `name` points at a string literal, and changing a literal is undefined behaviour (literals are read-only; on Linux it crashes). Fix: `char name[] = "bart";` makes an array holding a copy, which may be changed.
quiz.explain: The notebook's literal2.c and literal3.c show exactly this pair.

quiz.q: After `char a[] = "hello";` and `char *p = "hello";`, which line does **not** compile?
quiz.explain: C has no array assignment, so `a = "bye";` is a compile error. `p = "bye";` and `p = a;` store a new address in the pointer, and `a[0] = 'j';` changes our own array.

`strcpy(buf + 2, "ab")` writes 'a', 'b', '\0' at indexes 2, 3, 4: buf is "xxab\0xxx". Printing `buf` stops at index 4. `buf + 5` is "xxx". Replacing the '\0' at index 4 with '-' joins the two parts: "xxab-xxx".
The pointer visits every char and changes each 'a' to 'o'. When the loop ends, `p` points at the '\0' at index 6, so `p - w` is 6 (the length). `w + 3` is the string from index 3: "ono".
`end` points at the last char (index 7, 'd'). The loop prints indexes 7, 6, 5, 4 backwards: 'd', 'e', 's', 's'. Then `word[3] = '\0'` cuts the string after "str": length 3.

quiz.answer: `copy` has no room for the '\0' that `strcpy` always writes. It must be `char copy[strlen(src) + 1];`.
quiz.explain: Writing one char past the end is undefined behaviour, like too_small.c: it may seem to work, or silently overwrite another variable.

quiz.q: too_small.c has `struct t { char s[4]; int i; };`, sets `tmp.i = 99`, stores 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd' in `tmp.s[0]` to `tmp.s[3]`, then `tmp.s[4] = '\0';`. Afterwards it printed `tmp.i = 0`. Why, and why can we not say what it *must* print?
quiz.answer: "abcd" needs 5 chars, but `s` only has indexes 0 to 3, so `tmp.s[4]` is outside the array. Here the '\0' was written into the first byte of `i`, which follows `s` in memory, changing 99 to 0. Writing out of bounds is undefined behaviour, so the C standard does not say what happens; another compiler or layout could give anything (or crash).
quiz.explain: The fix is a bigger array: `char s[5];` for strings up to length 4.
After the first `strcat`, `s` is "abcd". The inner call in `printf` makes it "abcdef" and returns `s`; the outer call adds "!". Length 7, capacity still 12 (the declared size).

quiz.q: `char greeting[N] = "Good ";` and `char who[] = "morning";` What is the smallest `N` for which `strcat(greeting, who);` is safe?
quiz.explain: 5 + 7 = 12 characters, plus 1 for the '\0': 13. (The Fall 2014 final described this danger: a destination that fits its first string but not the joined one.)

"pea" is a start of "pear": it comes first. 'P' (80) < 'p' (112): "Pear" comes first. "pear" vs "peach": the first difference is 'r' vs 'c', and 'r' is bigger, so the result is positive and `< 0` is false (0). Equal strings give 0.

quiz.answer: `==` compares the address in `argv[1]` with the address of the literal, not the characters, so it is never reliably true. Use `if (strcmp(argv[1], "yes") == 0)` (and `#include <string.h>`).
quiz.explain: gcc says: "comparison with string literal results in unspecified behavior".

quiz.q: Using the notebook's compare.c, what does `./compare cat Category` print, and why?
quiz.answer: `cat comes after Category`. The first chars differ: 'c' (99) is greater than 'C' (67), so `strcmp` is positive. The rest of the strings does not matter.
quiz.explain: strcmp is case sensitive: it compares character codes, and all uppercase letters come before all lowercase letters.

write.prompt: Write your own `char *my_strcpy(char *dest, const char *src)` that behaves like `strcpy`: copy the characters of `src` and the `'\0'` into `dest`, and return `dest`. Walk both strings with pointers (no square brackets) and do not call any library function. Write a `main` that shows the copy is independent of the original, and that copies into the middle of an array.
write.explain:
`d` and `s` start at the two strings and move together. The loop copies one char per pass and stops when `*s` is the terminator, **before** copying it, so the line after the loop must write the `'\0'` itself (forgetting it is the classic bug). We move copies `d` and `s` so that `dest` still points at the start and can be returned. In `main`, changing `copy[0]` does not change `word`: they are two arrays. `copy` has 8 chars for the 7 of "pointer" plus '\0'. Copying to `line + 2` overwrites from index 2 and the new '\0' cuts off the dashes. Output:

```
$ ./w1
pointer Pointer
cd
ABcd
```

The notebook's short version `while (*dest++ = *src++)` does the same thing (the assignment's value is the char copied, and the loop stops after copying the 0); the longer form is clearer to write by hand.

rubric.item: pointer loop that stops at the `'\0'` of `src`
copies `*s` to `*d` and moves both pointers
writes the `'\0'` at the end of `dest`
returns the original `dest` (not the moved pointer)

pitfalls: Not writing the '\0' after the loop.
Returning `d` (which points at the end) instead of `dest`.
Making the destination array `strlen(src)` chars instead of `strlen(src) + 1`.

write.prompt: Modeled on Fall 2014 Q4 (the danger of `strcat`), without the heap. Complete `join` so that it puts `a` followed by `b` into `dest`, an array of `cap` chars. If the joined string and its `'\0'` would not fit, it must return 0 and **not** touch `dest`; otherwise it builds the string with `strcpy` and `strcat` and returns 1. The program should print `Happy Holidays` and then `too long for 16 chars`.

rubric.item: `strcpy(dest, a)` first (dest may hold garbage, so it cannot be `strcat`)
passes the capacity as `sizeof(greeting)` (16), from main where `greeting` is an array

pitfalls: Forgetting the + 1: "Happy " + a 10-char word would then overflow by one char.
Starting with `strcat(dest, a)`: `greeting` is uninitialised, so it is not a string yet.
Using `sizeof(dest)` inside `join`: `dest` is a pointer there, so that is 8.

write.prompt:
Modeled on Fall 2016 Q4 (which read lines from a file), using command line arguments instead. Write a complete C program `ordered` that decides whether its arguments are in dictionary order (case sensitive: use `strcmp`). Equal neighbours are allowed.

- With no arguments, print a usage message to standard error and exit with a failure status.
- First check every argument: if any argument is longer than 20 characters, write an error message to standard error and exit with a failure status.
- If the arguments are in order, print `arguments are in order` and exit successfully.
- Otherwise print `arguments out of order:` and then the **first** pair that is out of order, each on its own line indented by two spaces, and exit with a failure status.

```
$ ./ordered apple banana grape grape orange
arguments are in order
$ ./ordered apple grape banana peach orange
arguments out of order:
  grape
  banana
```

(Lab 5 of Day 16 tests this program: `./cdrill.sh check 16 5`.)

rubric.item: `int main(int argc, char *argv[])` with the right `#include`s (`<stdio.h>`, `<stdlib.h>`, `<string.h>`)
no arguments: message on `stderr`, non-zero exit
length check of every argument with `strlen(argv[i]) > 20` before any comparing; error on `stderr`, non-zero exit
loop over neighbours `argv[i - 1]`, `argv[i]` for `i` from 2 to `argc - 1` (no index past `argc - 1`)
out of order means `strcmp(argv[i - 1], argv[i]) > 0` (equal is fine); prints the first such pair in the required format and exits with failure at once
prints the success message only after the loop, exit status 0
compares with `strcmp`, never with `<` or `==` on the pointers

pitfalls: Using `>= 0` or `!= 0`: equal neighbours (grape, grape) would then count as out of order.
Printing `arguments are in order` inside the loop.
Testing `strcmp(...) == 1`: only the sign is guaranteed.
